title: The Zeigarnik effect: why unfinished tasks stick
description: You forget the shopping you finished but keep remembering the email you half-wrote. Psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik found that unfinished tasks cling to memory far better than completed ones — and you can use the effect on purpose.

body.heading: Waiters, orders and open loops
paragraphs: In 1920s Berlin, Zeigarnik noticed waiters who could recall long, unpaid orders in perfect detail — and forgot them the moment the bill was settled. Her experiments confirmed it: people remember interrupted tasks markedly better than completed ones, because the mind keeps an open task mentally 'on hold'.
The flip side is the 3 a.m. reminder loop: an unfinished task keeps resurfacing, which feels like stress but is really a filing system refusing to close a file.

body.heading: Close the loop on paper
paragraphs: You do not have to finish a task to quiet it — you have to give the loop a trusted next step. Writing down exactly what remains and what the next action is lets the mind file the task as handled-for-now; studies of planning show the mental rehearsal stops once a concrete plan exists.

And the effect cuts the other way for starting: beginning a dreaded task for just two minutes opens a loop your mind then wants to close, which is why starting small so often carries you further than motivation does.

takeaway: Unfinished tasks stick in memory — the Zeigarnik effect. Quiet them by writing the next step down, and exploit them by starting for just two minutes.
